books.section: Topic 5.8 Military Conflict in the Civil War
Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: General Winfield Scott, letter to General George B. McClellan (May 3, 1861)

stimulus.source_note: General Winfield Scott, letter to General George B. McClellan, May 3, 1861. Public domain; quoted as printed in 5 Steps to a 5, Chapter 15. Bracketed words are the book’s editorial note.
stimulus.text:
“We rely greatly on the sure operation of a complete blockade of the Atlantic and Gulf ports soon to commence. In connection with such a blockade we propose a powerful movement down the Mississippi to the ocean, with a cordon of posts at proper points, and the capture of Forts Jackson and Saint Philip [at New Orleans]; the object being to clear out and keep open this great line of communication in connection with the strict blockade of the seaboard, so as to envelop the insurgent states and bring them to terms with less bloodshed than by any other plan.”

—General Winfield Scott, letter to General George B. McClellan, May 3, 1861

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Scott writes that his plan would bring the South to terms “with less bloodshed than by any other plan.” This phrase suggests that Scott believed

options.text: the South would surrender without any fighting.
options.misconception: Scott plans a blockade and a river campaign; he expects pressure, not a bloodless surrender.

options.text: strangling the South’s supplies would avoid a bloody invasion.
the war would be over by Christmas of 1861.
options.misconception: Background: Scott was unusual precisely because he did not promise a quick war.

options.text: the navy alone could win the war.
options.misconception: Scott pairs the blockade with an army movement down the Mississippi, not the navy alone.

rationales.A: Scott plans a blockade and a river campaign; he expects pressure, not a bloodless surrender.
rationales.B: Background from the books: Scott was the one senior officer who warned the war would be long and hard.
rationales.C: Background: Scott was unusual precisely because he did not promise a quick war.
rationales.D: Scott pairs the blockade with an army movement down the Mississippi, not the navy alone.
rationales.general:
1. “Less bloodshed” is a comparison: Scott is weighing his plan against the alternative.
2. The alternative was a head-on invasion, army against army, which would cost many lives.
3. His plan instead squeezes the South’s trade and food until it gives in.
4. Background from the books: Scott alone among senior officers warned the war would be long and hard.
Remember: less bloodshed is a claim about method: squeeze, don’t storm.
